script:
1. DoubleTree, Tower of London — The opening kickoff

All right, Eagles fans—welcome to London! Today, we’re taking our road-game energy into a neighborhood of castles, riverboats, and nearly two thousand years of history. We’ll find a real connection to the founder of Pennsylvania, meet a Londoner who knew the importance of protecting his cheese, and get that Tower Bridge photo your friends back home are expecting. Keep the midnight green visible, keep your camera ready, and remember: traffic here can surprise an American. Use the crossings. Let’s move the chains—London edition!

Next: Walk west along Pepys Street, then south along Seething Lane to the garden. 2–3 minutes.

2. Seething Lane Garden — Protect the cheese

Stop near the Samuel Pepys bust.

Meet Samuel Pepys—pronounced “Peeps”—a navy administrator whose diary became an extraordinary eyewitness account of seventeenth-century London. He lived and worked here, and when the Great Fire threatened in 1666, he buried wine and Parmesan cheese to keep them safe. Now that’s a man who understood protecting the essentials. A Philly fan might grab the jersey, the tickets, and the tailgate supplies. Look for the carved paving stones telling his story. Before instant replays and social media, Pepys was recording the action, one remarkable day at a time.


Next: Continue south to All Hallows by the Tower. 2 minutes.

3. All Hallows by the Tower — Philadelphia’s London roots

Stop outside the church on Byward Street.

Eagles fans, this is our Philadelphia connection. William Penn, the founder of Pennsylvania, was baptized in this church and educated in its old schoolroom. Long before Philadelphia had a skyline, a stadium, or a cheesesteak debate, part of our home story was taking shape right here. All Hallows traces its foundation to the year 675, centuries before the Tower next door. And there’s another American connection: John Quincy Adams married here in 1797. Take a moment with this one. Across the Atlantic, a little piece of home is waiting.


Next: Use the marked crossing on Byward Street and follow the pedestrian approach toward the Tower’s western entrance. 4–5 minutes.

4. Tower of London — The ultimate home-field advantage

Gather in the public area outside the western entrance, clear of admission queues.

That fortress is the Tower of London, begun under William the Conqueror in the 1070s. It was a message in stone: the new king was here, and he intended to stay. Over the centuries, this place served as a royal residence, a prison, and a treasury. Think of those walls as the ultimate home-field advantage—although visiting teams had much worse problems than crowd noise. Today, the Crown Jewels are kept inside. We’re scouting the exterior on this walk; exploring the Tower itself deserves a separate visit.


Next: Continue to the riverside promenade at Tower Wharf. 2–3 minutes.

5. Tower Wharf — A river-city moment

Face the Thames, with Tower Bridge ahead.

Take a breath and look along the Thames—pronounced “Temz.” From here, London gives us a whole different view: water in the foreground, fortress walls behind us, and Tower Bridge just ahead. For anyone who loves Philadelphia’s waterfront, there’s something familiar about seeing a city from its river. Watch the boats, take in the skyline, and imagine trading your usual Delaware River view for this one. This is our first team-photo timeout. Get the Eagles gear in the frame—we want the folks back home to know who’s representing.

Next: Follow the riverside promenade east toward Tower Bridge. 4–5 minutes.

6. Tower Bridge — The highlight-reel photo

Stop at the north-bank viewpoint immediately west of the bridge.

There it is: Tower Bridge. And here’s your first London trivia win—this is not London Bridge. Despite its castle-like towers, Tower Bridge opened in 1894. Its two central roadway sections can rise to let tall vessels pass, making it a working piece of engineering as well as a world-famous landmark. That’s a pretty impressive opening in the middle—although we’d still like our offensive line to make a bigger one. Grab your photo here with both towers behind you. Midnight green, big smiles, and a London highlight worth sending home.


Next: Continue beneath the bridge’s north approach on the pedestrian route, following signs to St Katharine Docks. 4–5 minutes.

7. St Katharine Docks — The waterfront timeout

Stop at the west basin; keep this a short visit rather than circling the entire marina.

Welcome to St Katharine Docks, where our tour shifts from fortress mode into waterfront timeout. These docks opened in 1828, with a layout designed by engineer Thomas Telford. Today, boats, waterside restaurants, and cafés give the place a very different rhythm. After the crowds around the Tower, this is a good spot to slow down and pick a place you might return to later. Think of it as scouting the postgame gathering spot. For now, enjoy the harbor view—we’ve got one more defensive line to inspect before heading home.


Next: Return toward St Katharine’s Way and the Tower Bridge approach. Follow pedestrian signs west along Tower Hill, using marked crossings to reach the Roman wall beside Tower Hill station. 8–10 minutes.

8. Roman wall at Tower Hill — The original defensive line

Stop beside the surviving wall near the statue of Emperor Trajan.

Now we’re looking at a defensive line that predates football by a very comfortable margin. The Romans built London’s city wall around the year 200, and this is one of its substantial surviving sections. Look low down for the Roman stonework and bands of red tile; the wall was raised and altered in later centuries. That means you’re seeing layers of London’s history stacked together. Eagles fans appreciate strength in the trenches, and this city took defense seriously. Nearly eighteen centuries later, part of that line is still standing.


Next: Head west toward Trinity Square, then back to Pepys Street and the DoubleTree. 3–4 minutes.

9. Back at the DoubleTree — The victory huddle

And we’re back at the DoubleTree! In one neighborhood, we’ve found William Penn’s London roots, a diarist protecting his cheese, a royal fortress, a bridge that opens, a harbor, and a Roman defensive line. That’s a pretty strong stat sheet for a walk before the next meal. The best road trips give you more than a ticket and a final score—they give you stories you’ll bring home. Today, we added a few London stories to our Philadelphia collection. Get some water, check those photos, and—Go Birds!
